title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #211
gist: A roundup of five distinct bets: Amgen/AstraZeneca's tarlatamab Phase III win in small-cell lung cancer, the FDA's first-ever approval of a gene therapy (Ultragenyx's Fayuvi) for Sanfilippo type A, Lowercarbon's pitch for a planetary-scale 'Natural General Intelligence' model, TypeSafe's launch of Jev (a decision-only model claiming 20-200x speed and 40-400x cost advantages), and Thatch's $108M Series C at a $1B valuation on the thesis that ICHRA puts healthcare dollars in individuals' hands.

themes.theme: Tarlatamab Phase III in small-cell lung cancer

insights.claim: Amgen and AstraZeneca reported positive results from DeLLphi-305, a randomized Phase III trial of 563 extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer patients, where adding tarlatamab to durvalumab after chemo/immunotherapy significantly improved both overall survival and progression-free time versus durvalumab alone.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A positive randomized Phase III in a maintenance setting expands tarlatamab's addressable population beyond later lines and is a direct revenue catalyst for Amgen and AstraZeneca.
insights.quote: Amgen and AstraZeneca reported positive results from DeLLphi-305, a randomized Phase III trial involving 563 patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer.
insights.locator: (1) A Cancer Trial Gives Ben Wilson Reason for Hope

insights.claim: Tarlatamab works by physically connecting cancer cells bearing the DLL3 protein to the immune system's T cells so they attack, while durvalumab blocks one of the mechanisms tumors use to suppress that immune response, making the two mechanistically complementary rather than merely additive.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Validates DLL3-targeted T-cell engagers combined with checkpoint blockade as a template other oncology developers can copy into adjacent solid-tumor targets.
insights.locator: Tarlatamab connects cancer cells bearing a protein

insights.claim: Detailed survival numbers from the trial are not yet public and are expected the following month, so the announced 'positive' readout is directional rather than quantified.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A dated, unpriced data release is a tradable event: magnitude of the survival benefit, not its existence, is what will move the stocks.
insights.quote: The data won't come out until next month but this early indication is better than I could have hoped for.
insights.locator: The detailed survival numbers aren't public yet

insights.claim: Given the pace of progress in cancer treatments, therapies that merely slow cancer's spread are valuable because they can keep patients alive long enough to reach a later, more complete cure.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Reframes incremental-survival oncology assets as options on future curative therapy, arguing against discounting drugs that only extend life by months.
insights.quote: slowing cancer's spread and giving people more time might mean that they live long enough for a more complete cure
insights.locator: Given the pace of progress in cancer treatments

themes.theme: Fayuvi: first Sanfilippo A gene therapy

insights.claim: The FDA approved Fayuvi, Ultragenyx's one-time IV gene therapy that uses an AAV9 virus to deliver a working copy of the broken gene, making it the first treatment ever for Sanfilippo syndrome type A, with shipment expected within 30-60 days.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A first-in-disease approval with near-term shipping gives Ultragenyx pricing power in an untreated ultra-rare indication and a near-term revenue line.
insights.quote: On Thursday, the FDA approved Fayuvi, Ultragenyx's gene therapy and the first treatment ever for Sanfilippo type A.
insights.locator: (2) First Treatment for “Childhood Alzheimer's” Approved

insights.claim: In the pivotal trial, 17 treated children scored 23.5 points higher on a standard cognitive scale than 27 untreated children from a natural history cohort, with follow-up now stretching to nearly eight years.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Tiny-n trials against natural-history controls plus near-decade durability are becoming an acceptable approval path, lowering the trial cost of rare-disease gene therapy programs.
insights.quote: 17 treated kids scored 23.5 points higher on a standard cognitive scale than 27 untreated kids from a natural history cohort
insights.locator: In the pivotal trial, 17 treated kids

insights.claim: The FDA rejected this therapy last July over manufacturing issues even while explicitly calling the clinical data robust, and approval only followed after Ultragenyx fixed the plants and resubmitted.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Chemistry-manufacturing-controls, not efficacy, is the binding constraint on gene therapy approvals, so CRL headlines on manufacturing should be treated as timing delays rather than thesis breaks.
insights.quote: the FDA rejected it over manufacturing issues, even while calling the clinical data robust
insights.locator: Then last July, the FDA rejected it

insights.claim: The therapy was built by Haiyan Fu and Doug McCarty at Nationwide Children's more than a decade ago and licensed to Abeona, which ran out of money despite good data before handing it to Ultragenyx.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Capital exhaustion, not scientific failure, is the common death mode for rare-disease assets, which creates a recurring opportunity to buy orphan programs cheaply from distressed biotechs.
insights.locator: Haiyan Fu and Doug McCarty built the therapy

insights.claim: Because the gene therapy works best when given early, before neurological damage is done, universal newborn screening is the next required step for the treatment to reach its potential.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Screening infrastructure, not drug supply, will gate the commercial ramp of early-intervention gene therapies, making diagnostics an adjacent investable bottleneck.
insights.quote: It works best given early, before the damage is done, so the next thing that needs to happen is newborn screening.
insights.locator: It works best given early

themes.theme: Natural General Intelligence for the planet

insights.claim: Lowercarbon partner Ryan Orbuch argues that we do not know nearly enough about the planet, that the tools to collect that data now exist, and that the data should be gathered and put into a single model he calls Natural General Intelligence.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Signals where a leading climate fund is pointing its next wave of capital: planetary sensing and foundation models on environmental data.
insights.locator: (3) Natural General Intelligence

insights.claim: Only 27% of the ocean floor has been mapped with modern sonar, and much of that coverage is coarse and low resolution.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Quantifies the data vacuum that ocean-mapping, sensing and survey companies are being funded to fill.
insights.quote: we have mapped only 27% of the ocean floor with modern sonar, and much of that is coarse, low resolution
insights.locator: When Will O'Brien and I wrote about The Great Blue Frontier

insights.claim: Planetary modeling is structurally analogous to biology, where models have proven useful at making sense of enormous amounts of ever-changing data too complex for humans to grasp holistically, and the goal is to intervene in Earth systems the way medicine intervenes in bodies.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If the bio-model playbook transfers, expect the same value stack to form in climate: proprietary data collection first, then foundation models, then intervention products.
insights.locator: this problem is an awful lot like biology

insights.claim: Diogo Almeida, who helped develop the research behind ChatGPT and RLHF, spent two years building TypeSafe's model Jev, which takes information plus questions with predefined answer formats and returns decisions and probabilities in parallel rather than generating prose one token at a time.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A credible founder attacking the classification/decision layer suggests a wedge market that frontier chat models are structurally overpriced for.
insights.quote: Jev takes information and questions with predefined answer formats, then returns decisions and probabilities.
insights.locator: (4) ChatGPT & RLHF Co-Inventor Releases TypeSafe AI

insights.claim: TypeSafe claims Jev delivers 20-200x faster responses and 40-400x lower costs than frontier models on the decisions it is designed for, though these are company-reported numbers with third-party benchmarks not yet available.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If even directionally true, this compresses the economics of high-volume classification workloads currently billed to frontier-model APIs.
insights.quote: Almeida claims Jev produces 20–200× faster responses and 40–400× lower costs than frontier models on the decisions Jev is designed for.
insights.locator: Almeida claims Jev produces

insights.claim: Return on Tokens (ROT) is the right lens for enterprise AI spend, because a model that skips generating long explanatory answers for humans stops burning tokens on output that has no decision value.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Gives a metric for screening AI vendors and internal deployments: cost per decision, not tokens consumed or benchmark scores.
insights.quote: It seems like a smart way to increase companies' Return on Tokens (ROT)
insights.locator: It's not burning tokens writing long answers

insights.claim: If intelligence gets cheap and fast enough, developers will embed it into all the small decisions that previously required brittle rules or human review, such as routing support tickets, flagging suspicious transactions and scoring churn risk, a Jevons-paradox dynamic the company named itself after.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Supports the view that falling inference cost expands total AI spend rather than shrinking it, which is bullish for aggregate compute demand even as per-call prices collapse.
insights.quote: As it gets cheaper and more efficient, we'll use more of it. That's why they named it Jev, after William Stanley Jevons, of Jevons paradox fame.
insights.locator: The tools keep getting better!

themes.theme: Thatch, ICHRA and healthcare demand aggregation

insights.claim: Thatch announced a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation, with ARR growing nearly 7x over the past twelve months and more than 5,000 employers now on the platform.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Near-7x ARR growth at a $1B mark makes ICHRA administration one of the faster-compounding benefits-fintech categories to track for comparables.
insights.quote: Its ARR has grown nearly 7× over the past twelve months, and more than 5,000 employers now use the platform.
insights.locator: (5) Thatch Raises $108M Series C at $1B

insights.claim: Thatch's cap table combines venture investors The General Partnership, Index Ventures, General Catalyst and a16z with strategic investors Eli Lilly, ADP Ventures and Paychex, while Not Boring Capital has been an investor since 2022.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Payroll incumbents ADP and Paychex investing rather than building signals distribution partnerships over competition, and Eli Lilly's participation hints at pharma interest in direct-to-individual benefit dollars; note the author is a disclosed investor.
insights.locator: Investors include The General Partnership

insights.claim: Changing who controls healthcare dollars can change the healthcare system itself, because once individuals choose how to spend, providers and insurers must build offerings that compete for those dollars.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The investable claim is that defined-contribution health benefits force product competition in insurance, favoring carriers that build consumer-facing individual plans.
insights.quote: my thesis was that changing who controls healthcare dollars could change the healthcare system
insights.locator: When I wrote about Thatch last October

insights.claim: If someone can keep their insurer when they change jobs, the insurer has more reason to invest in keeping them healthy over time, because the payoff from prevention no longer leaks to a competitor.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Portability changes insurer incentives on preventive care and chronic-disease management, a structural tailwind for prevention and long-horizon care businesses.
insights.quote: if someone can keep their insurer when they change jobs, the insurer has more reason to invest in keeping them healthy over time
insights.locator: The bet is that insurers and providers behave differently

insights.claim: Thatch's model only works if it aggregates enough demand to persuade carriers to build better products, which attracts more people and pulls still better products out of the market, so scale rather than product quality is the gating variable.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Judge ICHRA platforms on covered-lives aggregation and carrier leverage, not ARR alone, since the flywheel does not start until the demand pool is big enough to move insurer product roadmaps.
insights.quote: Thatch needs to aggregate enough demand to persuade carriers to build better products, which could attract more people, which would pull still better products out of the market.
insights.locator: In order for Thatch to change the big, sclerotic
